title: The functional model and cell faults
summary: Thousands of physical defects can hit a memory, but a test engineer needs only a handful of **fault models**. This topic introduces the functional model of a memory and the faults of a single cell — and for each one, the shortest sequence of operations that detects it.
objectives: Name the three blocks of the reduced functional model and why faults are mapped to them.
Describe stuck-at, transition, stuck-open and data-retention faults with state diagrams.
Write the minimum sequence of writes and reads that detects each of them.

blocks.md: For testing, a memory is described by three blocks. Every defect — wherever it sits physically — shows up as wrong behaviour of one of them.

blocks.caption: Address decoder, cell array, read/write logic

spots.title: Address decoder
spots.md: Turns the address into one word line and one column selection. Its faults make the memory access the **wrong cell, no cell or several cells** — the *address-decoder faults* of Topic 6.

spots.title: Memory cell array
spots.md: The cells themselves. Faults of **one cell** (this topic) or between **two or more cells** (coupling faults, Topic 5).

spots.title: Read / write logic
spots.md: Sense amplifiers, write drivers, data registers. A broken sense amplifier makes a whole column read the same value — to the test it looks exactly like **stuck-at faults of the cells** in that column.

blocks.title: Fewer models, same coverage
blocks.md: Faults of the read/write logic and of the decoder can be **mapped** to equivalent faults of the cell array or to address-decoder faults. So a test that detects all **cell-array faults** and all **address-decoder faults** also detects the defects in the rest of the memory. That is the basis of every memory test.
A good cell is a tiny state machine with two states. Writing 0 (**w0**) always leads to state 0, writing 1 (**w1**) to state 1. Step through what goes wrong in a faulty cell:

steps.title: Good cell
steps.md: Both states can be reached from each other; each write ends in the written value.

steps.title: Stuck-at-0
steps.md: Whatever is written, the cell stays **0** (e.g. a short to ground). A test must **write 1 and read 1** — the read returns 0.

steps.title: Stuck-at-1
steps.md: The cell is always **1**. Detected by **write 0, read 0**.

steps.title: Up-transition fault
steps.md: The cell can hold a 1 but **cannot make the 0 → 1 transition** (e.g. a weak write path). The test must first put a **0** in the cell, then write 1, then read: **w0, w1, r1**.

steps.title: Down-transition fault
steps.md: The cell cannot make the **1 → 0** transition. Detected by **w1, w0, r0**.

blocks.title: Order matters already for one cell
blocks.md: A transition fault is invisible to *w1, r1* if the cell already held 1 — the failing transition never happened. The test must create the transition **on purpose**.

tabs.label: Stuck-open fault (SOF)
tabs.md:
An **open** in the cell's access path (a broken contact to the word line or the access transistor): the cell can be neither written nor read. What does a read return? Many sense amplifiers simply keep their **last value** — so the read returns the data of the **previous read**.

To catch it, the test must read the cell when the expected value is **different** from what the sense amplifier read just before — e.g. read a 0 from one cell, then read a 1 from the faulty one.

tabs.label: Data-retention fault (DRF)
tabs.md:
The cell accepts a value and returns it correctly — but **loses it after a while**, for example because one pull-up transistor is open and the node slowly leaks.

A quick test passes. To catch it, the test **writes, waits** (e.g. tens to hundreds of milliseconds), then **reads** — for both 0 and 1. MBIST controllers therefore support a **pause** step.

rows: the cell cannot be accessed; a read returns the previous read data
reads in a row that expect **different** values
the cell loses its value after some time
w0, pause, r0 and w1, pause, r1
blocks.caption: Single-cell faults and how to catch them

blocks.prompt: Practice: which fault explains the symptom?

items.text: w1, r1 passes, but w0, w1, r1 fails
passes a fast test, fails after a 100 ms pause

questions.text: Which blocks make up the reduced functional model of a memory? Select **all**.
A sense amplifier is broken and always outputs 0. To a memory test this looks like …
options: stuck-at-0 faults of the cells in that column
a transition fault of one cell

questions.text: Which sequence is guaranteed to detect an **up-transition** fault (0 → 1 fails)?
questions.explain: The cell must first be put in 0, so that w1 really makes the failing 0 → 1 transition.

questions.text: Writing 1 and reading 1 always detects an up-transition fault.
questions.explain: If the cell already held 1, no 0 → 1 transition happens and the fault stays hidden.

questions.text: A cell has a stuck-open fault and the sense amplifier keeps its last value. What does a read of that cell return?
options: The data of the previous read

questions.text: Why does a fast March test miss a data-retention fault?
options: The cell keeps its value for a short time; only a pause between write and read reveals the loss.
Retention faults only appear in ROMs.
March tests never read the cells.
